analysis.one_liner: Mandates two-person crews, trackside defect detectors, and higher fines for trains carrying hazardous materials.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2025 with bipartisan backing from six Republicans and five Democrats, the bill has sat without a single action in House committees since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tighten federal safety rules for freight trains carrying hazardous materials. It would require two-person crews, trackside detectors that catch failing wheel bearings and brakes, advance notice to state officials about what dangerous chemicals are moving through their communities, fewer trains blocking road crossings, bigger fines for safety violations, and a faster phase-out of older, less protective tank cars. It also charges each large railroad $1 million a year to fund training for local firefighters and emergency responders. The bill is a direct response to the 2023 Norfolk Southern derailment in East Palestine, Ohio, which spilled hazardous chemicals into a town on the Pennsylvania-Ohio border.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near rail lines, especially in towns along routes that carry oil, chemicals, and other hazardous freight; local firefighters and emergency crews who currently lack money and information to prepare for a chemical spill; and rail workers who would gain a required second crew member on long trains.

how_it_helps.text: Requires DOT to write rules requiring advance notice to state and Tribal emergency response officials about hazardous materials moving through their areas, plus a written gas discharge plan [S2][S3].

Requires all Class I railroads to install hotbox detectors — trackside sensors that catch overheating wheel bearings, a known cause of derailments — at least every 10 miles on hazmat routes, with clear rules for what crews must do when one triggers an alert [S3].

Writes a two-person crew requirement (a certified conductor and a certified engineer) into federal law for freight trains, with narrow exceptions, and bars the exceptions for trains carrying toxic-by-inhalation materials or very long trains [S3].
Raises maximum civil penalties roughly tenfold — for example, from $75,000 to $750,000 per violation of hazardous materials transport rules — with fines scaled to a carrier's income [S2][S3].
Bars railroads from using older DOT-111 tank cars, widely faulted in past derailments, to haul flammable liquids starting May 1, 2027, regardless of train makeup [S3].
Charges each Class I railroad a $1 million annual fee to fund grants for local emergency response training, and doubles a separate training grant program to $4 million a year [S2][S3].

Requires shippers and railroads to reduce or eliminate blocked road crossings, and directs DOT to set limits on train length and weight, speed restrictions, track standards, and maintenance rules [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The large freight railroads (CSX, Norfolk Southern, Union Pacific, BNSF) and their shareholders bear the direct costs — new equipment, second crew members, larger fines, and the $1 million annual fee — and rail customers and consumers could see some of it passed through in freight rates. Owners of older tank cars would have to retire or retrofit them.

drawbacks.text: The bill's costs are real and recurring: hotbox detectors roughly every 10 miles, a legally required second crew member, more frequent qualified inspections, and tenfold fines all add operating expense that railroads can pass to shippers and, ultimately, to prices consumers pay [S2][S3].

Railroads argue two-person crew mandates raise costs without proven safety gains, since modern locomotives and automated inspection technology can substitute for crew members; the bill itself preserves pilot programs for automated rail inspection rather than banning the technology [S3].

The crew requirement includes a broad exception: operations that ran with smaller crews at least a year before enactment can apply to continue if the Secretary finds equivalent safety, so the mandate's real-world reach depends heavily on future regulatory decisions [S3].
Benefits are probabilistic — derailments like East Palestine are rare but catastrophic — while the compliance costs land every day, making it hard to weigh them dollar-for-dollar.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is strongest where past disasters exposed gaps: hotbox detector spacing, real-time hazmat notification to communities, tank car phase-out, and adequately funded first-responder training address failures documented after the East Palestine derailment. The two-person crew mandate is the most contested piece, with thinner evidence tying it to fewer accidents and the largest price tag, and the bill's own exception for existing small-crew operations softens it. On balance the bill targets the largest carriers, exempts most small railroads, and its costs are modest relative to the industry's profits, but critics fairly note that cost will partly show up in shipping prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure and Science committees, then sent to the railroads subcommittee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor action since February 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Deluzio introduced the Railway Safety Act of 2025 on February 4, 2025, joined by Reps. LaLota (R-NY), Rulli (R-PA), and Garamendi (D-CA) as original cosponsors [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and, additionally, to the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology [S1][S5].
It was then referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials, and the public record shows no further action since [S5].
Eleven members cosponsored the bill, six Republicans and five Democrats [S4].

The bill requires the Transportation Secretary to report on implementing the recommendations in the NTSB's 2024 report on the Norfolk Southern derailment and hazardous materials release — the East Palestine disaster that prompted this legislation [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the large freight railroads: no detector mandates, no crew-size requirement, no higher fines, and no $1 million annual fee have taken effect because the bill has not advanced out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship splits six Republicans and five Democrats, and two Republicans joined as original cosponsors, though no member has had to vote on it yet [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Class I freight railroads (CSX, Norfolk Southern, Union Pacific, BNSF)
industries.note: The bill would impose recurring costs on the biggest railroads — trackside detectors every 10 miles on hazmat routes, two-person crews, more rigorous inspections, fines up to ten times current caps, and a $1 million annual fee for first-responder training. Fewer derailments and better-funded local fire departments are public benefits the industry's costs buy, which is why the industry's interest runs against the bill. It has sat in committee, so none of these costs have taken effect.

industries.industry: Rail tank car owners and oil/chemical shippers using DOT-111 cars
industries.note: The bill ends the use of older DOT-111 tank cars for flammable liquids by May 2027, forcing owners to retrofit or retire them. These cars were implicated in past explosive derailments, so the cost falls on equipment owners while the protection goes to towns along the routes.

Carriers with under 400,000 employee work hours and under $40 million in revenue, running slow trains on non-main track, are exempted from the two-person crew rule, though some small railroads could still face inspection and detector obligations on hazmat routes.

industries.industry: Rail safety equipment suppliers (defect detector and inspection technology)
industries.note: Mandated detector installation and a $22 million grant program for detector effectiveness would create demand for wayside detection and inspection equipment; the bill preserves automated inspection pilot programs.

analysis.trajectory: With only a referral to subcommittee, no scheduled hearing or markup, and no visible vehicle for floor action, the bill is following the path of most House bills: it is likely to stall through the 119th Congress unless a derailment or committee attention revives it. Its bipartisan cosponsorship gives it more standing than a purely partisan bill, but the previous Congress's version of this legislation also died without floor votes in the House despite passing a Senate committee.
